title: Graduated Traffic Operator with Safety Curve Constraints
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary:
Implement a Graduated Traffic Operator (GTO) that drives canary rollouts and A/B experiments using safety-curve guardrails rather than fixed thresholds. The GTO provides declarative traffic steps, dynamic deceleration, and an automated rollback path based on both system and semantic signals. The goal is to reduce surprise regressions during model waves while maximizing safe exposure velocity across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Motivation / Background:
Existing canary tooling at Redwood is step-based with hard thresholds (e.g., error_rate > X). That leads to brittle rollouts for LLM workloads where quality regressions are noisy and sometimes delayed. We need an engine that reasons over trend direction, confidence intervals, request cohorts (shadow vs production), and aggregated prompt-set regressions to take more nuanced actions (pause, decelerate, rollback, or continue).

Goals:
- Declarative rollout spec that supports percentage ramps, time windows, and shadow probes.
- Safety curves: continuous guard function that maps metric deviation and statistical confidence to allowable traffic growth rate.
- Automatic rollback and staged fallback to compatible model variants when safety curves indicate sustained regressions.
- Region- and tier-aware routing so enterprise customers on Dedicated can opt stricter curves.
- Integrations: console telemetry, alert hooks, GitHub PR links for rollouts, and canary evaluation dashboards.

Proposed rollout DSL (example):

rollout: 
  name: graduated-release-2026-03
  target_model: model:v2.7
  steps: 
    - duration: 30m
      target_percent: 5
    - duration: 45m
      target_percent: 20
    - duration: 2h
      target_percent: 50
  shadow_probe: true
  safety_curve: 
    metric_weights: {latency_p95: 0.4, client_error_rate: 0.3, eval_regression: 0.3}
    max_growth_rate: 2.0  # multiplier applied to previous step percent per evaluation interval
    deceleration_policy: "curve-based"
  rollback_policy:
    sustained_violation_minutes: 15
    fallback_variant: model:v2.6-quant

Note: DSL above is illustrative and intentionally kept simple; final schema will be JSON/YAML friendly and validated by server.

Safety Curve Details:
- The safety curve converts multi-metric deltas into a single safety score S in [0,1]. Growth rate permitted for the next window = base_growth * f(S) where f is a monotonic function that clamps to [0, max_growth_rate].
- Use Bayesian online change detection for early sensitivity and compute a posterior confidence interval before taking irreversible actions.
- Metric sources: runtime telemetry (p95, p99, qps), error taxonomy (server vs client vs model-evaluation failures), synthetic evals (prompt-set score deltas), and user-facing regression indicators (support triage events).

Rollback and Fallback Behavior:
- Soft pause: reduce traffic growth to zero and extend current step if safety score crosses warning boundary for 1 evaluation window.
- Hard rollback: revert traffic to baseline and switch route to fallback_variant after sustained violation window.
- Shadow-only probing: when in doubt, route a sampled percentage to model:v2.7 as shadow to collect semantic eval signals without impacting users.

Observability and Controls:
- Console: per-rollout timeline with safety score, metric contribution breakdown, and decision log entries.
- API: endpoints to start/abort/pause/resume rollouts and to simulate rollouts against historical telemetry.
- Audit: each automated action must create an immutable audit record with the causal metrics and computed confidence.

Acceptance criteria:
- Engine accepts rollout spec and executes a 3-step rollout in staging with shadow probes enabled.
- Safety curve correctly reduces growth when synthetic evals show a semantic regression on curated prompt set (test harness).
- Auto-rollback triggers and switches to fallback_variant after configured sustained violation in at least two independent metrics.
- Console exposes decision timeline and links to the evaluation prompt set that triggered the decision.

Trade-offs and open questions:
- Complexity vs explainability: curve-based decisions are more subtle but harder to reason about than simple thresholds. We will provide a deterministic \"explain\" endpoint that returns the contributing metric weights and intermediate calculations for each decision.
- Compute cost: continuous Bayesian change detection and per-rollout evaluation increases CPU/DB load. Plan: sampling and adaptive evaluation frequency (reduce cadence when rollout is stable).
- Ownership: runtime will own enforcement hooks; console will own visualization/controls. The policy engine lives in the control plane so it can operate across dedicated and private clusters.

Security and compliance considerations:
- All decision logs are recorded with request-level hashes; no raw PII should be stored.
- For Private customers, policy engine must be deployable into their control plane; default metrics collection will be configurable via connectors.

Deliverables / next steps:
- PRD linked below and a narrow prototype that runs a shadow probe and computes a safety score over a 24h window.
- Follow-up tickets: real-time metric adapters, rollout DSL validation, console timeline UI, and audit log export.
